State of Punjab vs. Surjit Singh

115, 302, 120B

Supreme Court of India

The accused was alleged to have abetted the commission of an offense punishable with death or imprisonment for life. The prosecution claimed conspiracy and abetment to commit murder, leading to charges under Section 115 read with Section 302 of the IPC.

Whether the charge of abetment under Section 115 IPC is sustainable when the principal offense was not committed Sufficiency of evidence regarding criminal conspiracy to abet murder

The Supreme Court analyzed the ingredients of abetment under Section 115 of the IPC, noting that abetment of an offense punishable with death or imprisonment for life, if the offense is not committed in consequence of the abetment, carries specific penal consequences. Upon reviewing the evidence, the Court found the links in the chain of circumstantial evidence insufficient to prove the charge beyond reasonable doubt.

Attempted Murder / Abetment

State of Punjab vs. Madan Lal

379, 411

Supreme Court of India

The accused was prosecuted for the theft of a motorcycle under Section 379 and for dishonestly receiving stolen property under Section 411 of the IPC. The trial court and appellate courts evaluated the recovery of the vehicle at the instance of the accused.

Whether the recovery of the stolen vehicle was proved beyond reasonable doubt Whether the ingredients of Section 379 IPC were satisfied

The Supreme Court noted that the consistent testimony of official witnesses coupled with the recovery of the stolen property from the possession of the accused sufficiently established the guilt under Section 379 and Section 411 IPC.

State of Punjab vs. Gurmit Singh

457, 380, 411

Supreme Court of India

The accused was charged with lurking house-trespass by night and theft in order to commit an offence punishable with imprisonment, under Sections 457 and 380 of the IPC. The prosecution alleged that the accused broke into a dwelling house during the night and stole valuable property.

Whether the ingredients of lurking house-trespass by night under Section 457 IPC were satisfied. The reliability of circumstantial evidence and recovery of stolen property under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.

The Supreme Court evaluated the evidence regarding the nocturnal break-in and the subsequent recovery of stolen articles at the instance of the accused. Finding the chain of circumstances complete and the testimony of recovery witnesses credible, the conviction under Section 457 and 380 IPC was upheld.

Burglary and Theft

Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj & Anr.

465, 467, 468, 471, 120B

Supreme Court of India

The case arose from allegations of fabrication and creation of forged power of attorney documents and sale deeds to illegally transfer immovable property belonging to the complainant. The trial court and appellate forums dealt with the scope of forgery concerning valuable securities and property.

Whether the ingredients of forgery under Section 463 and punishable under Section 467 of the IPC are made out against the accused. Whether a charge under Section 467 can be sustained without direct and cogent evidence proving the execution of the forged document by the accused.

The Supreme Court held that unless the ingredients of forgery—specifically the making of a false document with intent to cause damage or injury—are strictly established, no conviction under Sections 465, 467, 468, or 471 can be sustained. The prosecution failed to establish the foundational facts connecting the accused directly to the fabrication of the documents.

Forgery and Fraud

Malkhan Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2003) 5 SCC 746

457, 376

Supreme Court of India

The appellants committed lurking house-trespass by night by forcefully entering the dwelling house of the prosecutrix and subjected her to gang rape while threatening her family members.

Evidentiary value and necessity of a Test Identification Parade (TIP) in a case of nocturnal house-trespass and sexual assault Sustainability of conviction under Section 457 and Section 376(2)(g) of IPC based primarily on the credible testimony of the prosecutrix

The Supreme Court held that identification in court is substantive evidence and failure to hold a test identification parade is not necessarily fatal to the prosecution. The prosecutrix had sufficient opportunity to see and remember the features of the intruders who committed lurking house-trespass by night, rendering her identification fully reliable.

Lurking House-Trespass by Night and Gang Rape

State of Maharashtra v. Sayed Mohammed

379, 34

Supreme Court of India

The accused were intercepted while fleeing with stolen property. The trial court convicted them under Section 379 read with Section 34 of the IPC, which was upheld through the appellate hierarchy.

Whether the circumstantial evidence conclusively proved the commission of theft under Section 379 IPC Whether joint liability under Section 34 IPC was rightly invoked

The Court held that recovery of the stolen articles immediately after the incident from the possession of the accused, coupled with their failure to offer any plausible explanation, establishes the offense of theft beyond reasonable doubt.

Theft
